caption:
You already know what happens next. That is the entire trick.

An anticipation hook is a shot of something one second away from resolving — a fuel hose still in the tank as the car pulls away, a leaning pole over a parked car, an axe suspended above a boulder. Your brain refuses to scroll until it sees the ending.

Here is the part most people miss: the hook does not have to relate to your topic at all. Its only job is to buy you the three seconds you need before your actual content starts.

Why it works, mechanically:

→ Instagram ranks on watch time. The first three seconds decide whether anyone ever reaches your point.
→ Mosseri has said about half of Instagram videos are watched with no sound. Your hook has to work on mute — movement and tension in frame one, not a clever line.
→ Tension is the only thing that survives a thumb moving at full speed.

How to use it: two or three seconds of hook at the very front, then cut hard into your real content. The tension carries the viewer across the cut, and by the time they realise the subject changed, they are already watching.

Most people spend an hour on the caption and zero seconds on the first frame. That is backwards. The caption is read by people who already stopped.
